lesson.title: Clock & Calendar Gym
lesson.subtitle: Wie viel Uhr ist es? — telling time, halb past and all

hook.title: Half Past Seven Is Half TO Eight
hook.content: One clock, two mentalities. Formal German reads it straight: Es ist drei Uhr — it is three o'clock, exactly like English. But the half hour betrays the older mind: halb acht is NOT half past seven — it is 'half of the way TO eight', seven-thirty. English 'half past seven' counts from the hour that just passed; German halb acht counts toward the hour that is coming. Once you catch the logic, the whole colloquial clock opens: Viertel nach sieben (quarter after seven), Viertel vor acht (quarter to eight).

footnotes.title: halb's Hidden Twin
footnotes.content: halb ↔ half — the f/v→b shift in action, one of the quiet family words. Es ist halb acht: the same 'half', counting in the opposite direction.

pattern.title: Two Clocks, One Answer
pattern.content: Formal (always safe): Es ist sieben Uhr dreißig — seven thirty, digits read aloud. Colloquial, moving forward: Viertel nach sieben (7:15), halb acht (7:30!), fünf nach halb acht (7:35). Colloquial, approaching: Viertel vor acht (7:45), zehn vor acht (7:50). Questions: Wie viel Uhr ist es? (literally 'how much clock is it?') or the idiom Wie spät ist es? ('how late is it?'). Calendar glue: gestern, heute, morgen slot before the time: Morgen um acht Uhr — tomorrow at eight. At? = um. Um acht Uhr trinken wir Kaffee.
pattern.linguist_note: halb acht's 'half toward' logic once existed in English too — archaic texts say 'half seven' the same way. English standardized on 'half past'; German kept the older directional count.

exercises.prompt: Trap drill: 'Es ist halb acht.' What time is it?
exercises.meaning: halb acht = half (of the way) TO eight = 7:30
exercises.explanation: German counts the half toward the coming hour; English 'half past' counts from the finished one. One habit flip.

exercises.prompt: Match each time phrase with its English meaning — the clock and the calendar:
exercises.target_answer: Es ist drei Uhr, Viertel nach zwölf, Viertel vor acht, Morgen um acht, am Wochenende, im Sommer, im Winter
exercises.meaning: it is three o'clock, quarter past twelve, quarter to eight, tomorrow at eight, on the weekend, in the summer, in the winter
exercises.explanation: The clock phrases carry the shift twins; the calendar phrases borrow the clock's own little words: am = an dem, im = in dem — contractions, not new words. nach = after (moving forward), vor = before (approaching), um = at. The colloquial clock is prepositions.

exercises.prompt: Ask the question: '_____ viel Uhr ist es?' (How much clock is it?):
exercises.meaning: Wie viel Uhr ist es? = What time is it?
exercises.explanation: wie — the how-word whose root is why's — drives the clock question: 'How much clock is it?' Count along: zählen is tale's twin, and die Minute is the clock's smallest tale — hundert of them to the hour.

exercises.prompt: 'Gestern ___ ich früh aufgestanden.' (Yesterday I got up early — auxiliary needed)
exercises.explanation: aufstehen is motion (up!) — sein opens the bracket, and with a fronted gestern the verb still holds position 2.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'Tomorrow at eight we drink coffee'
exercises.target_answer: Morgen um acht trinken wir Kaffee
exercises.meaning: Tomorrow at eight we drink coffee
exercises.explanation: Time stack (Morgen um acht) in position 1, verb glued to 2, subject to 3 — V2 with a full calendar.

summary.outcome: Tell time formally and colloquially — and never mistrust halb again.

use_example.german: Morgen um acht trinken wir Kaffee.
use_example.english: Tomorrow at eight we drink coffee.

summary.takeaway: halb acht is half-toward-eight; nach pushes forward, vor pulls up to, um pins the hour.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Gestern habe ich… Story Drills — narrate a whole weekend in Perfekt sentences from taught words.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "The clock / o'clock is here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Die Uhr ist heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in Clock & Calendar Gym.

uhr.etymology_derivation: Loan-cognate of hour (Latin hōra via French), and a distant doublet of Jahr and year (PIE *yóh₁r̥). German alone turned it into the word for the clock itself. [wiktionary]

halb.context_translation: It is half past seven (halfway to eight).

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

heute.etymology_derivation: Literally 'on this day': heu- is the he- of here/him, and the old ending hid Tag (day). English's own twin hēodæġ died out — today won. [wiktionary]

zwölf.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *twalif — 'two left over', the exact tw → zw twin of twelve. [wiktionary]

wochenende.context_phrase: Am Wochenende fahren wir an den See.
wochenende.context_translation: On the weekend we go to the lake.
wochenende.etymology_derivation: Woche + Ende — the modern compound arose in the 19th century as a calque of English weekend; Woche is the twin of week (k → ch) and Ende the twin of end. [wiktionary]

sommer.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *sumar — English summer is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

winter.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wintruz — English winter is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

hundert.context_phrase: Ein Jahr hat nicht hundert Tage.
hundert.context_translation: A year does not have a hundred days.
hundert.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaradą 'hundred-count' — the twin of English hundred. [wiktionary]

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin minūta — the same Latin loan as English minute. [wiktionary]

zählen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *taljaną, the causative of the tal-root — the same family as English tell and tale; the initial t became z, as in two, zwei. [wiktionary]

grillen.context_phrase: Im Sommer grillen wir im Garten.
grillen.context_translation: In summer we grill in the garden.
grillen.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English grill — a modern loanword kept almost unchanged, with a Swiss synonym grillieren. [wiktionary]

stau.context_translation: There is a traffic jam on the motorway.
stau.etymology_derivation: From Low German stouwe (weir), a back-formation of stauen (to dam up); the page compares English stow — traffic stowed on the motorway. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
